content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper introduced CLANS, a continual learning (CL) method mixing reinforcement learning with a growing-architecture approach to CL. CLANS leverages RL to determine the number of neurons to add to each layer in response to a new task in a task incremental setting (task ID needed at training time, multi-head outputs). Then it leverages network masking on the extended topology to determine which parameters to adapt to the new task. Then a second step of adaptation is applied recursively to past tasks to enable backward transfer. A replay buffer is used to determine task similarity and to perform the backward adaptation.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
STRENGHTS

(+) The method is designed in such a way  in which both forward and backward transfer are naturally obtained

(+) The empirical analysis considers a good number of related models from the family of architectural approaches to CL

WEAKNESSES

(-) Simply put, the proposed method is an overkill which goes against any motivation subsuming the introduction of continual learning methods. The architectural complexity, computational and memory costs of the method are way beyond what is considered in line with reasonable in CL. It is important to remark that the main motivation of lifelong/continual learning is making continuous adaptation and acquisition of skills scalable. CLANS has huge computational demands, for tiny advantages in terms of predictive accuracy and knowledge transfer. 

(-) While the paper presents some results about the computational costs of the method, which exceed the day in several cases (as compared to hours in other methods), there is no similar level of transparency for the memory cost. I am not referring to the number of network parameters (available in Table 2), but rather to the size of the replay buffers needed by the method. The paper is unclear about this but by reading between the lines it seems that the validation set of each task is kept in the buffer. This is a quite large replay buffer and given that it is used not only to determine task similarity but also to adapt the network for backward transfer, I wander if much of the advantage of CLANS stems in fact from the fact that it can reuse such very large replay buffers. In this sense it would be interesting to see the performance of the SGD-type network with a replay based on the same buffer used by CLANS. 

(-) The empirical analysis shows minor quantitative advantages of the method, in return for its huge complexity. In addition to that, no confidence intervals are provided, despite the trials being repeated 5 times, so I guess one can at least report the std. This would certainly help to understand how significant are the differences between CLANS and the related models. The very same reasoning applies to the ablation study in Figure 4: the effect of the ablated components is not striking. In particular fixed sized addition of neurons does not seem to deplete substantially the performance against the version with the RL agent. Also here the standard deviations might provide further insight into significance of the difference.

(-) The method is assessed in a reasonably “easy” task incremental setting. Aside from the fact that would be interesting to see the performance of the method on more realistic single-head incremental settings, it is not clear how the new heads are wired to the existing architecture when these are added after arrival of a new task. Is the new head fully connected to the last layer of the network? Or is it rather connected to only the “newly added neurons”?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper has some novelty in the fact that it attempts to bring in together several techniques available in different works in literature. However the overall quality of the work is quite limited by the fact that forward/backward transfer are not obtained by some novel insight or theory. Rather, they are some very straightforward consequence of the growing + heavy replay choices. Nothing new in that, but huge computational demands. If the paper intends, as written in the appendix, to propose a method amenable for mobile applications, these are definitely not the right design choices.  Clarity is also not at the best, with several design choices not clearly discussed (including the heavy use of replay and its impact).
content.summary_of_the_review: The overall low level of novel insight and the methodological choices, that fall way outside of the perimeter of what CL typically considers a realistic resource consumption, makes this paper leaning on the negative side of acceptance. Forward and backward transfer effects are strengths of the work, but these are obtained by means that I can hardly define consistent with the typical CL scenarios.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.

display_title: The motivation and contribution of CLANS

content.title: The motivation and contribution of CLANS
content.comment:
**a) Response to Motivation:** \
-- In this study, we focus on addressing the knowledge transfer problem in continual learning through neuron selection. The motivation is that the similar neuron selections in different tasks may indicate the existence of shareable knowledge that can be transferred to both old and new tasks. We use the RL algorithm because we believe that RL enables dynamic signals to scale the network as well as affect the neuron selection of a new task, where the selection depends not only on new knowledge in the new task but also on previous tasks. In contrast to existing RL algorithms, we treat task similarity and selection similarity as the environment state to boost the learning of RL. And we also use a masking mechanism to prune the task network, which provides us with a more compact task network (cf. Table 2). Indeed, our method needs more computing resources due to the expansion optimization within RL environment. If we make a fixed expansion like BNS and PGN, our method can be very fast but could result in more memory cost of task network and slight accuracy loss (cf. Response c) of Review 1). \
--As for accuracy performance, to the best of our knowledge, most network adaption-based methods as well as our baselines WSN and RCL are to freeze the learned parameters of earlier tasks to address the CF issue. Compared to regularization-based methods (e.g., EWC and IMM), these works have achieved remarkable accuracy on several benchmark datasets due to the freezing operation. So, it is hard to make a further huge improvement as we expected. Recall the BWT and Trans, especially for Trans, CLANS provides us with more achievements for knowledge transfer by a large margin. In particular, the positive results of BWT on three datasets show that our CLANS surpasses even the learning accuracy in the context of single-task learning. \

**b) Response to Replay Buffer:** \
-- In fact, we do not use the replay buffer to alleviate the forgetting issue during training for the new coming task as the replay-based method did. In contrast to some recent studies such as BNS for knowledge transfer, we only use the replay buffer to obtain the similarity scores of different tasks. Moreover, the similarity needs to be calculated only once before training a new task (cf. Algorithm 2). \
--As for the size of the replay buffer, we follow BNS and use the validation set as the replay buffer. We also did an additional experiment to reduce the buffer size to 5%, and the accuracy of CLANS on TinyImageNet is 39.12%, which is still better than the baseline with a slight decrease. \
**c) Response to the 'std':** \
--We have reported the std in our Appendix part. As for the ablation study, we have the following results regarding ACC(%). \

| Dataset      | CLANS-R      | CLANS-F      | CLANS-K      |
| ------------ | ------------ | ------------ | ------------ |
| PMNIST       | 97.82(0.025) | 97.83(0.137) | 98.07(0.408) |
| RMNIST       | 96.67(0.051) | 97.72(0.016) | 97.89(0.209) |
| CIFAR100     | 70.55(0.148) | 70.80(0.771) | 71.22(0.421) |
| TinyImageNet | 39.03(0.196) | 39.14(0.104) | 38.03(0.195) |

**d) Response to the ‘head’:** \
--We follow the baselines, e.g., HAT and WSN, and use a multi-head classifier for each dataset. That is to say, our head is fully connected to the output of the last hidden layer. We also claimed this point in our implementation setup on page 7.

content.title: Thanks for the rebuttal
content.comment:
I have appreciated the response of the authors to my concerns and those from the other reviewers. There is clearly a shared concern among us as regards the computational and memory complexity of the approach that, in my view, stems from attempting to situate this work in a typical CL setting. I won't repete the comment in my review, but the CL community is highly motivated by specific challenges that require a careful trade-off between the incremental learning methodology, the catastrophic forgetting control, the forward-backward transfer and the computational aspects.  I believe that this work excels in some of these aspects, but at excessive costs on others (namely computational). In this sense the rebuttal does not add much to the discussion.

However, I do find interesting the comment of Rev mFmB about heterogenity: it could be the case that this work can find its proper placement at the crossroads between CL and AutoML, where the heterogeinity of the tasks calls for incremental model selection/architecture search. My suggestion in this sense is to carefully consider whether this might be the setting to showcase the model (and where computational costs are certainly much more accepted).

About the replay buffer: I know the method does not use it to replay, yet the approach needs to store the data like a replay based approach. The problem with replay approaches, among the others, also hold for this work: namely having to keep too much data to be scalable and keep assessing task similarity on a fixed and potentially outdated snapshot of data representative for the tasks. I would still like to see how a replay method with as much buffer size as your method is allowed to use would behave. I suspect the performance would be in line with the SOTA.

Lastly about the head: I have rechecked the paper and you indeed state that multiheads are used (and I already got this point). My question was specifically whether the newly introduced head connects to all neurons in the preceeding layer or not. Because figure 1 suggests it does not. It suggests the newly introduced task is only connected with a subset of the neurons. Then I would be glad to know how such a subset is determined. If instead this is not the case, it would be nice to know what is the rationale of connecting densely to the previous layer when the methodology is based on determining what subnets contribute to a task.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a reinforcement learning based method for task-incremental learning.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
Using RL to help continual learning is interesting if we can see tangible benefits. 
The paper is fairly easy to read. 

Weaknesses
Novelty is significant considering there are already existing RL based continual learning methods and the proposed system is not compared with the most recent method experimentally. In the related work, the comparison is also sketchy. 

You mentioned two RL based continual learning system RCL and BNS. Why didn’t you include BNS as a baseline, which is more recent (2021) than RCL (2018)?  I just checked the BNS paper. It seems that your accuracy numbers are much lower than those in the BNS paper. 

Since you claimed that your system can do knowledge transfer, why didn’t you use the two datasets in BNS that have a lot of shared knowledge. The amount of positive transfer in your current results is too small, almost negligible, which can hardly justify the claim. 
The accuracy improvement compared to HAT, SupSup and WSN are very small (mostly < 1%). Considering the standard deviations, it is hard to claim there is any significant improvement.  

There are several other systems that perform network expansion without using RL. They select neurons or parameters through pruning or other methods. For example, the following two systems should have been compared experimentally, 
(1)	Yan et al., DER: Dynamically expandable representation for class incremental learning, CVPR-2021.
(2)	Hung et al., Compacting, Picking and Growing for Unforgetting Continual Learning, NeurIPS-2019.
DER is designed for class-incremental learning, but it can be easily used for task incremental learning. 

The running speed of the proposed system is very slow, which is expected as RL is usually slow. Please compare with those pruning based methods (1) and (2). 

In the main text of the paper, you didn’t give the size of the validation data. I found it in the Appendix that you are using 20% of the training data of each class as the validation set, which is saved like the replay data. This number is way too big compared to the number used in a typical replay-based method. For example, for CIFAR100, you need to save 100 samples per class, but a typical replay method save at most 20 per class. 

AlexNet is not a particularly strong backbone. ResNet would have given much better results. Why didn’t you use ResNet?

Novelty is limited as there are existing RL based methods and the proposed system is not compared with the most recent RL based continual learning method experimentally. 
The code has been submitted.

content.title: The details about our baselines
content.comment:
**a) Response to 'BNS':** \
 --We totally agree with this concern. When we started this study, we indeed recognized that BNS is a more related and recent method that provides several actions to configure the task network and leverages RL to expand the network. However, we cannot find any source codes for implementation (the provided link in the paper is still empty). In addition, we had requested the source code but did not receive any response before finishing this study. To be fair, you can find that all the baselines are implemented according to official sources. Besides, since we cannot find any implementation details of CL setting in BNS, it could be not fair to compare our model accuracy to the BNS’s directly. We make a special note here. That is: our solution is significantly different from BNS. BNS can only expand the network with a fixed size while the task network complexity is not considered. In addition, the actions in BNS make knowledge transfer by modifying the trained parameters, which could significantly disturb the current (even future) task. But like BNS, we also mainly compare HAT to evaluate the effectiveness of our CLANS. \
  **b) Response to 'Knowledge Transfer':** \
--The core work of our study is striving to make knowledge transfer during continual learning. As for forward knowledge transfer, we find that our method has a significantly better improvement than baselines in terms of ‘Trans’. Overall, the performance on RMNIST and TinyImageNet has a positive value (‘Trans’), which demonstrates that the task training in our CL environment even outperforms the task training in an independent learning environment. As for the backward transfer, we find that our method indeed successfully makes newly learned knowledge to promote the old tasks (cf. BWT). \
 **c) Response to 'Network Expansion and Pruning in DER':** \
-- The goal of DER is to tackle the class-incremental learning tasks. It is also based on HAT which uses the mask method to prune its feature extractor. In our study, we also employ the mask operation to prune the task network. The most difference is that our selection (pruning) is not only conditioned on current task optimization but also upon the similarity measurement in RL environment. More importantly, DER also employs the replay buffer (i.e., memory) to preserve part of the previous samples that will be co-trained together (cf. Eq.(3) in the paper) in each task learning. In contrast, we do not co-train the samples from the replay buffer. We also use the source code of DER (cf. https://github.com/g-u-n/pycil and https://github.com/Rhyssiyan/DERClassIL.pytorch) to conduct the results of TinyImageNet in our CL setting. We find that its accuracy is just 38.7% and it obtains obvious negative values of BWT, which is significantly lower than ours. In practice, the pruning method will provide a more compact network for each task, but the pruning process still takes much time.\

**d) Response to 'The size of validation data':** \
--In our study, we do not use the replay buffer to help address the forgetting issue of old tasks, which is significantly different from replay-based methods. We only use the replay buffer to provide the similarity scores to initialize the initial state of RL. We also did an additional experiment to reduce the buffer size to 5%, and the accuracy of CLANS on TinyImageNet was 39.12%, still better than the baseline with a slight decrease.

**e) Response to 'AlexNet':** \
--We follow the HAT and choose the AlexNet for a fair comparison, as HAT achieves the best accuracy among baselines.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes Continual Learning solution via Adaptive Neuron Selection (CLANS), a method to tackle the problem of catastrophic forgetting in continual neural networks. CLANS treats network neurons as a knowledge pool from which neurons can be selected and dynamically expanded. Neuron selection uses and expandable gating mechanism, while neuron expansion uses reinforcement learning. The method also allows knowledge transfer through enrichment of neurons in the knowledge pool. Experiments on four benchmark datasets show that the method is competitive in terms of metrics such as overall accuracy, forward and backward transfer.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The paper proposes a novel method that aims at learning the best architecture for a set of continual tasks, which considers not only tackling catastrophic forgetting but also encouraging knowledge transfer in both directions. The technical design of the method is sound in the sense that it selects and expands selectively according to the task at hand. 
- The paper is well written, easy to follow and aligned with the literature in the area.
- The experiments consider a good range of SOTA methods in the area, and measure both accuracy and knowledge transfer.

Weaknesses:
- The main weakness that I see in this paper is in the experimental results presented in Table 1. From these results, it seems that the proposed method outperforms all baselines by a very small margin on average, in both average accuracy and backward transfer specifically. Can you report deviations across the 5 runs? 
- Another weakness that I see in this paper is in regards to the method itself. From my understanding in Section 3, backward transfer will only occur only conditioned on the neurons selected for the target task. However, an alternative solution is to select neurons (and expand) neurons for the target task in parallel to trying to achieve enrichment of previous tasks. How would this alternative perform compared to your proposed method? Although from Table 1 I appreciate the positive backward transfer results achieved for some datasets, I also see that these results are only marginally better than baselines, similar to what happens with overall accuracy. Would this alternative of encouraging both new task learning and backward transfer in parallel make the results better?

After rebuttal
- The computational cost of the method is quite remarkable, as pointed by other reviewers
- The deviation results show that the method does not achieve substantial gains in terms of accuracy or backward transfer
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is very clearly written and well presented. The quality of the paper is high, since the method is adequately explained and the experimental results fairly presented. I consider that the novelty of the method is high as it considers using reinforcement learning to learn the best architecture for a current task while also trying to re-use knowledge from previous tasks. The reproducibility of the paper is good as the authors provide data and code in the supplementary material.
content.summary_of_the_review: Apart from the couple of weaknesses listed as part of this review, for which I am looking forward to the response of the authors, I consider that this paper presents a novel method for dynamic network expansion in continual learning. The novel part of the proposed method is that, different from previous work, it uses reinforcement learning to learn to make such expansion. I also consider interesting the fact that the authors aim at achieving knowledge transfer beyond forgetting. Based on this, I see this paper as a borderline accept, which I may reconsider based on the response of the authors to my concerns.

content.title: Accuracy performance and implementation
content.comment:
**a) Response to 'deviation' and performance accuracy:** \
--We had provided the deviations as shown in Table 6 in Appendix C.3.1. Thanks a lot. In this study, we mainly focus on solving the knowledge transfer problem with adaptive neuron selection. The inspiration is that incremental knowledge acquisition could have a corrective effect on early cognition, although the learning of new tasks heavily depends on the perspective of existing experience. Since most network adaption-based methods are to freeze the learned parameters of earlier tasks for addressing the forgetting problem, these works such as WSN and RCL have achieved remarkable accuracy on several benchmark datasets such as MINIST. In contrast to regularization-based methods such as EWC, it is hard to make a further huge improvement as we expected. Recall the BWT and Trans, especially for Trans, CLANS provides us with more achievements for knowledge transfer by a large margin. In particular, the positive results of BWT on three datasets show that our CLANS surpasses even the learning accuracy in the context of single-task learning. \
**b) Response to ‘backward transfer’:** \
--Yes, the backward transfer will only occur when the current task has been well-trained. Indeed, we have tried to make backward transfers during training for the current task. But training time is not acceptable as more tasks are coming. So, we give up this alternative. Like human cognitive processes, transferring knowledge to old tasks is a complex but significant task in recent continual learning. The reason is that the backward knowledge transfer requires changing the trained network architecture for each of the old tasks. If we perform backward knowledge transfer while training the current task at the same time, it will also lead to memory cost concerns. Certainly, we recognize that knowledge transfer in continual learning should be more similar to the process of human learning; because old knowledge is likely to be updated at any time in the process of learning new knowledge.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents CLANS, a reinforcement learning based continual learning system that is composed of three components, Task Network, Neuron Expander, and Neuron Selector. CLANS is evaluated on four benchmarks, PMNIST, RMNSIT, CIFAR, and TinyImageNet, demonstrating competitive performance in terms of average accurate and backward and forward transfer.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- I appreciate the systems approach to continual learning this paper adopts. 
- CLANS is sound and all constituent components are well motivated and effective.
- Experiments are comprehensive covering a number of baselines, metrics, and ablation studies.

Weakness:
- Some decisions were stated but not justified. For example, why was the Jensen-Shannon Divergence (JSD) used to measure between the current task and earlier tasks? And why was the cosine distance used to measure the similarity score between the task T_t and the task T_i after j−1 iterations.
- The number of parameters was only compared to EWC, RCL, and HAT. Table 1 (or another table) should list the number of parameters of all methods under study.
- The major drawback of CLANS is the time for training and inference where in some instances it may take up to 25x (excluding DEN and RCL). The papers should explicitly state a breakdown of the time spent per component/step and highlight potential avenues for improvement.
- What about heterogeneous tasks?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- The paper is well-written, clear, and easy to follow.
- While most individual components of CLANS are not novel, the proposed system in totality is.
- All details of the experiment are provided as well as the code.
content.summary_of_the_review: In light of the assessment, strengths, and weakness above, this paper is an interesting contribution to continual learning and demonstrates strong empirical performance and would be a good contribution to the conference if the authors address the weaknesses mentioned above.

content.title: The details of the experiments
content.comment:
**a) Response to 'JSD and Cosine distance':**  \
--We use the common metric JSD to measure the similarity between two data distributions [1] while cosine is a common metric to measure the representation (embedding) similarity. First, most existing studies such as RCL usually use random values as the RL’s initial state. In contrast, we use the data distribution similarities as the initial state to boost the learning of RL optimization. Correspondingly, we choose JSD to measure the similarity of data distribution. However, the similarity scores regarding the distributions of different task data are fixed and cannot further provide a dynamic signal to help the training of neuron selection and expansion. Moreover, we consider that similar tasks could have similar neuron selection (or layer embedding). Thus, during our task learning, we turn to measure the similarity of different tasks’ layer embeddings via cosine metric. In sum, our RL environment is not only conditioned on task similarity but also selection (i.e., layer embedding) similarity.  
\[1] Niu S, Wu J, Xu G, et al. Adaxpert: Adapting neural architecture for growing data[C]//International Conference on Machine Learning. PMLR, 2021: 8184-8194. \
**b) Response to 'The number of parameters':** \
-- Table 2 reported the total allocated parameters after training all tasks. And other methods such as SGD, IMM-mean, IMM-mode are based on the regularization principle, where the neural architecture will not be changed throughout the continual learning. Therefore, the total number of parameters in these methods is similar to that of EWC. As for PGN, the total parameters for four datasets are: 1.2M, 1.2M, 8.6M, 8.8M  \
**c) Response to 'Training and inference time':** \
--We recognize that our method takes much time, mainly due to the RL setting. We also discuss this limitation and future direction in our Appendix part (cf. E.5 in Appendix). When we remove the RL part and expand each task network with a fixed number of neurons (i.e., CLANS-F). The total time and accuracy performance are:

| Dataset      | Total time | ACC           |
| ------------ | ---------- | ------------- |
| PMNIST       | 0.86h      | 97.83(±0.137) |
| RMNIST       | 0.75h      | 97.72(±0.016) |
| CIFAR100     | 0.48h      | 70.80(±0.771) |
| TinyImageNet | 2.03h      | 39.14(±0.195) |

We can find that CLANS-F performs worse than HAT except on TinyImageNet, which further suggests that our RL settings do help in learning a range of tasks. Furthermore, the goal of our RL in CLANS is not simply to expand the task network. The decision to extend is also influenced by the selection similarity of the old tasks (see Eq. (5) in our paper), which can provide a positive signal to perform knowledge transfer. \
**d) Response to 'Heterogeneous tasks':** \
-- Yes, tackling heterogeneous tasks has recently become more important in the CL context. Our CLANS is a simple search-like RL that makes it easy to dynamically select useful neurons or filters. For example, we can use our RL to select model A for task A but pick a different network architecture for task B that is totally different from task A. However, we also consider the similarity measurement to be the largest bottleneck. Institutively, the heterogenous tasks may be different in regards to the data distribution. However, we consider that heterogeneous tasks also contain rich, shareable knowledge that can be transferred across heterogeneous tasks. Therefore, our current work turns to the adoption of efficient NAS for addressing similar and dissimilar tasks based on knowledge similarity measures. We believe that CLANS provides us with a proactive effort to focus more on knowledge transfer between different tasks, especially for heterogeneous tasks.
